ai-winter: A time when people stopped giving money to AI research, because AI did not do what people promised. There were AI winters in the 1970s and around 1990.
artificial-intelligence: A computer program that does things that usually need human thinking, like seeing, talking, translating, or making choices. Most AI today learns from examples.
attention: In a transformer, the way the AI looks at all the other words to decide which ones matter most for each word.
audience: The people who will read, see, or use your work.
axon: The long part of a neuron that carries the signal away from the cell body, toward other neurons.
back-translation: Translating a translation back to the first language, to check it. If the meaning changed, something went wrong.
bias-number: In a neuron, an extra number that is always added to the total. It does the same job as a threshold. (The word “bias” has another meaning too: being unfair. See Unit 4.)
cellular-automaton: A row or grid of cells. Each cell is a color, like black or white. At each step, every cell changes by following the same rule, which looks only at its neighbors. More than one is called cellular automata.
chatbot: An AI program that you talk to with words. You type or say something, and it answers.
computer-program: A list of steps that a computer follows. Apps and games are computer programs.
computer-vision: AI that finds things in pictures and video, like faces, signs, or people in the street.
conditioning: Learning to connect two things that happen together. Ivan Pavlov’s dogs learned to connect a sound with food, so they drooled when they heard the sound.
context: The facts around your question: who you are, what the answer is for, and what you already know. A chatbot cannot guess these, so you tell it.
context-window: All the words a chatbot can read at one time. In a chat, it holds your old messages too. That is why a follow-up question works. A new chat starts with an empty context window.
data: Information, like pictures, words, numbers, or sounds. An AI learns from data.
dataset: A big collection of examples that an AI learns from, like pictures with labels.
deep-blue: A chess computer made by IBM. In 1997, it beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. It used rules that people wrote, and it checked about 200 million chess positions every second.
dendrite: One of the short branches of a neuron. Dendrites take in signals from other neurons.
diffusion: A way to make a picture: start with noise, then remove a little noise at a time, again and again, guided by words. A neural network guesses which part is noise.
draft: A first try at a piece of writing. You will change it to make it better.
edge: A place in a picture where it changes fast from dark to light. Edges show where things begin and end.
eliza-effect: When people feel that a computer understands them, but it does not. It is named after ELIZA, a chatbot from 1966.
emergence: When many simple parts work together and make something bigger and more complicated, which no one planned.
estimate: A quick answer that is close, but not exact. You can use it to check if an answer makes sense.
fact-check: To find out if something is true, using good sources.
feedback: Comments that tell you what is good about your work and what to make better. Good feedback is kind, specific, and helpful.
filter: A small grid of numbers that slides over a picture. At each spot, it multiplies and adds. A filter can find edges or make a picture blurry.
follow-up-question: A question you ask after an answer, to make the answer better. For example: “Explain it in simple words” or “Give me an example.”
format: What an answer should look like: a list, a table, 3 sentences, simple words, or a certain language.
gallery-walk: Walking around the room to look at everyone’s work and leave feedback notes, like visitors in an art gallery.
gpu: A computer chip first made for video games. It can do thousands of small math problems at the same time, so it is very good for training neural networks. GPU means “graphics processing unit.”
hallucination: When AI writes something false as if it were true, like a book or a court case that does not exist. The AI sounds just as sure as when it is right.
hint: A small help that shows you the next step, but not the answer.
hype: Big promises and excitement, more than the facts show.
image-generator: An AI that makes a new picture from words. Many image generators use diffusion.
input: A number that goes into a neuron or a program. In a picture, each square can be an input: 1 for black, 0 for white.
judge: In the Turing test, the person who asks the questions and decides which player is the machine.
key-word: A word that a program looks for to decide what to do.
label: The right answer that a person attaches to an example, like “cat” on a picture of a cat. An AI learns from examples and their labels.
large-language-model: A transformer trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next word. Chatbots like ChatGPT are built on large language models. People often call them LLMs.
lateral-reading: Checking a fact by opening new tabs to see what other sources say, instead of reading only one page. “Lateral” means “to the side.” Professional fact-checkers do this.
learning-curve: A graph that shows how you get better with practice. The time or the number of mistakes usually drops fast at first, then more slowly.
low-resource-language: A language with not much writing online for AI to learn from. AI usually makes more mistakes in these languages.
machine-learning: A way to make AI. People do not write the rules. They give the computer many examples, and the computer finds the patterns by itself.
neural-network: A kind of AI made of many small parts that work a little like brain cells. Each part does a tiny bit of math. A neural network learns from examples.
neuron: A cell that sends signals. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. A neuron fires (sends a signal) only when the signals coming in add up to enough.
noise: Random dots with no picture in them, like the static on an old TV.
overfitting: When an AI memorizes its training examples instead of learning the real pattern. It does very well on the training data but worse on new data.
pattern: Something that is the same, or repeats, in many examples.
perceptron: The first artificial neuron that could learn. Frank Rosenblatt built it in 1958. It multiplies inputs by weights, adds them, and fires if the total passes a threshold.
persona: A character that someone pretends to be. You can tell an AI to use a persona, like “Act like a 15-year-old student.”
pixel: One tiny square of a picture. A computer stores each pixel as a number. In a black-and-white picture, 0 is black and 255 is white.
plagiarism: Turning in someone else’s words or ideas as your own. Turning in AI writing as your own, when the assignment does not allow it, is plagiarism too.
prediction: A best guess about something you do not know yet. A prediction can be wrong.
product: The thing you make in a project, like a flyer, a study guide, or a plan.
prompt: What you type to tell an AI what you want. A good prompt has a task, context, and a format.
prompt-log: A list of every prompt you used in a project, and what you did with each answer.
random: With no pattern, so you cannot guess what comes next.
revise: To change your work to make it better, often after feedback.
rubric: A chart that shows how your work will be graded.
rule: An exact instruction that a computer follows: “If this happens, do that.” In a normal computer program, a person writes the rules.
source: Where a fact comes from: a book, a website, a news story, or a person.
style: The way a picture looks: a photo, a cartoon, a watercolor painting, pixel art.
synapse: The tiny gap between two neurons. Chemicals carry the signal across it. When you practice, the synapses you use get stronger.
task: The job you want the AI to do, like “explain,” “give me 3 ideas,” or “make a quiz.”
test-data: New examples that an AI never saw during training. We use them to check what the AI really learned.
threshold: The number that the total must pass for a neuron to fire.
token: A word or a piece of a word that a chatbot reads and writes. For example, “playing” might be two tokens: “play” and “ing.”
training: Showing an AI many examples so it can fix its weights. After each mistake, the weights change a little.
transfer-learning: Starting from an AI that already learned something, then teaching it a new job with a few new examples. It is much faster than starting from nothing.
transformer: A kind of neural network, first shared by Google scientists in 2017. It uses attention to connect the words in a sentence. It is the T in GPT.
translate: To change words from one language to another, with the same meaning.
turing-test: A game Alan Turing described in 1950. He called it the imitation game. A judge chats in writing with a person and a machine. If the judge cannot tell which one is the machine, the machine passes.
understand: To know what something means, not only what it looks like. Whether AI can understand is a question people still argue about.
weight: A number that says how much an input matters to a neuron. A big weight means the input matters a lot. A negative weight means the input makes the neuron less likely to fire. When a neural network learns, it changes its weights.
